lines.text: Isaac Newton put on a disguise and spent his nights in London's roughest taverns, hunting a forger.
The forger, William Chaloner, had stood up in Parliament and mocked him as incompetent.
You see, coins were real silver, so people shaved the edges and spent them at full value.
The baker clipped it. The tailor clipped it. By the tavern, it was the size of a button.
By 1695, a bag of silver money weighed barely half what it should.
So in 1696, England handed the whole mess to Newton.
But how do you stop a thief who only takes a sliver?
Newton went after the biggest crook first. By 1697, Chaloner was in jail.
Then Chaloner paid the star witness to flee to Scotland, and walked free.
So Newton spent two more years in disguise, one informant at a time.
In 1699, the jury took minutes. Guilty of high treason.
You see, his Mint melted the old money down and struck new coins by machine, with ridges all around the edge.
Shave a ridged coin, and the ridges vanish. Everyone can tell.
It's the seal on a new jar. You can't sneak a scoop without breaking it.
Today, an American quarter has no silver at all. Not since 1965.
Yet it still has a hundred and nineteen ridges.
Newton's lock never came off. There's just nothing inside worth stealing.
